newsitem.title: UK: EMU expectations exceed reality, markets vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: EMU expectations exceed reality, markets vulnerable.

text.p: Financial markets have placed their bets on convergence towards European monetary union (EMU) but analysts warn that expectations are exceeding reality and trouble could well lie ahead.

"This is a classic time for a massive correction," said David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns. "We are seeing the tail-end investors coming in, the market has got very over-speculative, frothy and over-mature...it is ripe for a correction."
With all the good news apparently priced in, particularly in the case of Italy, the big underlying risk going into next year is that growth fails to take off, analysts said.

Countries are assuming they will hit the Maastricht 3.0 percent budget deficit to GDP ratio on the back of strong growth next year, but the drum tight fiscal policies put in place to hit the fiscal target means growth will tend to be suppressed.

"If strong growth fails to materialise next year the Bundesbank is going to get a lot more EMU-phobic if we are heading for the prospect of missed targets," Bear Stearns said. "They don't want a soft euro."

It is not just question marks over Italy that are causing investors to take a second look, a call from former president Giscard d'Estaing for a French franc depreciation this week to revive growth has reopened the franc-fort debate.

"What we have seen in the past few days is significant," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International. "France is obviously a key part of EMU and now we seem to getting increasing concern about the weakness of the economy...and about time too."
Other government officials such as Gaullist National Assembly speaker and former anti-Maastricht campaigner Philippe Seguin have backed d'Estaing.

The big danger is that if the market gets a suspicion that there is any kind of wavering on franc-fort the franc could be hit extremely hard. The market has been nervously selling the franc since d'Estaing made his comments.

"Now the franc is under pressure there is going to be a knock-on effect," Stamenkovic said. "France is part of the core and if the market doubts the commitment to franc-fort they will start to shift their attention to the vulnerable currencies like the lira and peseta."
But with overseas investors only holding around 12 percent of French debt the convergence euphoria has really been played out in Italy, Spain.

Analysts said there is a danger that the market views Italy and Spain together but the two are very different. Spain has a much more sustainable fiscal position, a more stable currency and a stable government.

If the market sells both Italy and Spain in a shakeout the likelihood is that Spain would recover fairly quickly. "If there is a shakeout it will be primarily in the Italian lira and BTPs (Italian government bonds)," said Nick Parsons, currency strategist at Banque Paribas.
Italy is most vulnerable because in order to sell the idea of a EMU to a sceptical public, Germany needs to exclude Italy, he said. "On balance we believe Spain will be there but Italy will not."
The longer it takes for growth to pick-up the more likely it is that EMU will be delayed because it will be much harder for the German authorities to sell the idea domestically, analysts said.

"In 1998 when Germany celebrates the 50th anniversary of the deutschemark, the rock upon which German post-war prosperity has been built, the German public will be need to be convinced of the argument of abolishing it in six months time," Parsons said.
